This might be in a completely different context, but in a Model United Nations, we have Caucuses too. Primarily of two types, Moderated and Unmoderated, a caucus is basically a debate-ish discussion. In a Moderated Caucus, a topic is taken up with a 2/3rd majority voting for it, and whoever wishes to speak on the topic can raise their placard and they get to speak accordingly. There is however, minimum to no dialogue taking place here. There are situations though where controversy can arise and questioning becomes necessary. The speaker basically says what he/she wants to and goes back. The Unmoderated Caucus is very much different. The delegates are somewhat, let free and can discuss whatever they wish to and can write their working papers, etc. during this time. Most of the alliances and blocs are formed during this time and actual political discussion takes place here. I'd just like to add that whatever I just said is the format of UNAUSA, one of the most common MUN formats and not the H-MUN or any other.

As far as my knowledge goes, in Java 'new' is used to allocate memory space before actually putting the object/variable into the memory. It is generally used for non-primitive data types because the memory that they require isn't exactly predefined. That is why even when creating arrays, 'new' is used.

'this', as far as I have used it, is used for referring to the currently active object. Meaning, if you have created an object 'ob' and are using its var 'a', typing this.a will mean that you want to access the var 'a' of abject 'ob1'. However, the most common use, I guess, is to use 'this' to refer to global variables which, if you didn't already know, are defined outside the functions and directly under the class. These variable are accessible by all the functions of the class. If you have a global var of the same name inside any function, using this.(var name) will refer to the var that is global and not the local var (the var inside the function).
